implementation_notes: Two library realizations cover Java. libGDX's scene2d ships the packaged form: 'Stage has an act method that takes a delta time since last frame. This causes the act method on every actor in the scene to be called, allowing the actors to take some action based on time' - Actor.act(float) is the per-object step and the Stage is the collection and driver. JavaFX ships the JDK frame hook instead: 'The class AnimationTimer allows to create a timer, that is called in each frame while it is active. An extending class has to override the method handle(long) which will be called in every frame', with the frame timestamp shared by all timers. What replaces the classic structure: either the framework walks the objects (libGDX) or you walk a List<Updatable> yourself inside handle(long) (JavaFX) - the interface plus list form is the hand-written fallback and needs no base class beyond that interface. The handle timestamp is nanoseconds, so dt comes from subtracting the previous frame and clamping.
pitfalls: AnimationTimer.handle runs on the JavaFX Application Thread: blocking work freezes the UI, and start()/stop() issued from another thread are delegated asynchronously.
The timestamp is nanoseconds on an arbitrary time base: subtracting two readings gives dt, but the first frame and any pause produce a spike - clamp it.
Mutating the actor list (Stage.addActor/removeActor) inside act() changes the walk and can skip actors; add and remove at a defined point of the frame.
libGDX's act() also drives the Action system: calling it is optional, but without it actions and enter/exit events never happen - do not half-adopt the walk.
